stumbles.quote: That figure only holds when the pre-tokenizer splits on whitespace alone.
stumbles.why: "That figure" is ambiguous and the 21% setup is only implied; it also appears before the pre-tokenizer is introduced. The next sentence, "Ettin's tokenizer spends 376 tokens per abstract on the same set," gives no retrained-table count to compare against.

stumbles.quote: Ettin's tokenizer spends 376 tokens per abstract on the same set.
stumbles.why: It comes right after the whitespace-only caveat, so it reads as if it applies only to that condition. The baseline is never tied to the 21% or the 8%, and the retrained table's per-abstract count is missing.

stumbles.quote: The pre-tokenizer accounts for most of the difference.
stumbles.why: The 'difference' is unclear, and the text never says what pre-tokenizer the 21% setup uses beyond 'whitespace alone'. 21% vs 8% is implied but not stated.

stumbles.quote: Oskar asked on 2026-11-06 whether "we [could] create an entirely custom domain Ettin model with custom token table ... for life sciences".
stumbles.why: Oskar is never introduced, and the quote is elided and edited.

stumbles.quote: Training models on the new table is the subject of a separate experiment, lifesci-ettin
stumbles.why: It refers to an experiment I can't see, with no explanation of its status.

stumbles.quote: Retraining the vocabulary helps only if the pre-tokenization changes with it.
stumbles.why: This overstates the result, because the text itself says the retrained table still saves 8% with the GPT-2 pre-tokenizer.

point: A PubMed-retrained 50K BPE vocabulary cuts token counts by about 21% against Ettin's tokenizer, but only if the pre-tokenizer is also changed to whitespace-only. With Ettin's GPT-2 pre-tokenizer the saving is only 8%.
